newsitem.title: THAILAND: Amnuay was successful banker before entering polit.
newsitem.headline: Amnuay was successful banker before entering polit.

text.p: Amnuay Viravan, who quit as Thai deputy premier and finance minister on Thursday after less than seven months in the job, gave up a successful career as a banker to enter politics.
Amnuay resigned after a series of conflicts with political rivals within the six-party coalition government of prime minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, political sources said.
The straw that broke the camel's back for Amnuay was a decision by the cabinet this week to reverse his plan to raise excise taxes on three products.

The move against Amnuay's plan was spearheaded by Deputy prime minister and industry minister Korn Dabbaransi, viewed as a rival and a leader of the second-largest party in the ruling coalition, Chart Pattana.

Amnuay, a non-elected politician, was chosen by Chavalit for the coveted finance job amid quiet dissatisfaction within the premier's New Aspiration Party and the Chart Pattana headed by former premier Chatichai Choonhavan.

Most analysts praised Amnuay's performance as he struggled to reverse Thailand's worst economic slump in over a decade. The economy is in a severe downturn with growth officially seen slowing to 5.9 percent from 6.4 percent posted last year.

The ailing finance sector is over-exposed with loans to the depressed and cash-strapped property sector. Exports have turned sluggish, the baht has come under speculative attacks and the stock market is at an eight-year low.

Analysts said his limited success in curing the economic malaise was partly due to disunity in Chavalit's coalition, especially rivalry in economic policies with the Chart Pattana, which runs the key industry and communications ministries.

Among Amnuay's key policy measures were hefty cuts in the current and 1997/98 (Oct/Sept) fiscal budgets as the slowing economy sharply cut tax revenues, and his ambitious state rescue packages for ailing finance and property sectors.
Amnuay, an advocate of fiscal discipline and conservative economics, took over the finance portfolio last November with a respectable record.

Although he was former Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa's deputy in charge of foreign trade and international economic policy, he was not part of the inner circle empowered to set key budget and monetary policies.
The Banharn administration presided over the economic slump which began in mid-1996.
Amnuay, 65, has been a government economist, corporate executive, banker and cabinet minister during an illustrious 39-year career.

He rose to national prominence during his 18-year public service, first as finance adviser to former Thai military strongman Sarit Thanarat in the early 1960s and in the mid-1970s as permanent secretary for finance, the top civil servant at the ministry.

His public service ended in the aftermath of a military coup in 1976, and he fell victim to a subsequent right-wing purge of liberal government officials that persuaded the soft-spoken economist to spend 11 years in the private sector.
Between 1981 and 1992, Amnuay was chief executive of giant industrial group Saha-Union Plc and later joined Bangkok Bank Plc as executive chairman of the biggest Thai commercial bank.

Amnuay's experience included a stint as head of the Board of Investment (BoI) that promoted foreign investment, and as chairman of a government think-tank, the National Economic and Social Development Board (NESDB).
He entered national politics in 1992, quitting a comfortable job at Bangkok Bank to help former army chief Chavalit launch his New Aspiration Party.
Amnuay formed his own 18-seat Nam Thai (Thai Leaders) Party in September 1994, representing a constituency in northeast Khon Kaen province. He later left the party and it disbanded.
